key_insight: Gliding-mammal-inspired wing and tail shapes create distinct aerodynamic trade-offs, with broader membranes boosting lift and integrated or flat tails improving different control modes.
engineering_relevance: The study offers design guidance for bioinspired morphing aerial robots by linking morphology to lift, drag, stall behavior, and pitch/roll/yaw authority.
method: CFD simulations isolated aerodynamic effects of representative patagium and tail/uropatagium morphologies.
Three patagium shapes were compared under controlled flow to assess lift, drag, stall, and pitching moment.
Tail/uropatagium variants were tested in baseline, symmetric-deflection, and asymmetric-deflection cases to evaluate longitudinal and lateral control.
evidence_signal: The abstract reports comparative CFD evaluation of three patagium configurations and three tail configurations, showing morphology-dependent differences in lift, drag, stall response, and control authority.
watch_item: The conclusions are based on controlled computational conditions, so real-flight performance may differ once structural flexibility, unsteady motion, and full-scale body interactions are included.
paper_title: Patagium and tail morphology shape aerodynamic performance and control authority in gliding-mammal-inspired wings
